issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the method and results sections were generated from randomized dummy data rather than observed participant responses. Any statistical tests, effect estimates, hypothesis evaluations, or conclusions drawn from these data are not empirically meaningful. This invalidates the current results as evidence about replication success or the extension.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.description: The manuscript gives mutually incompatible statements about study status. It says results are based on simulated data, but elsewhere states that data collection was launched and completed before analyses. These contradictions make it impossible to know whether any real data exist, whether the reported analyses are hypothetical or final, and whether the preregistered plan was actually followed.
issues.quote: We first pre-registered the experiment on the Open Science Framework (OSF) and data collection was launched later that week. ... all studies were pre-registered with power analyses reported in the supplementary, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.description: The participant section reports detailed demographics for a dataset that was generated by Qualtrics rather than collected from actual human participants. These values are not interpretable as sample characteristics and should not be presented as such. Doing so can mislead readers into treating simulation output as empirical participant information.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: Key sample characteristics needed to evaluate external validity and reproducibility are missing, including geographic origin and participant compensation for the planned replication. This omission is especially important because the design differs substantially from the original and because payment/incentive structure is central to donation behavior.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified ... Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The manuscript states only that there were no exclusions, but provides no plan or report for handling incomplete responses, failed attention checks, duplicate MTurk submissions, partial item nonresponse, or survey dropouts. For an online study, these are important sources of bias and should be prespecified and reported.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.description: The power analysis is based on the smallest original main effect of intervention, but the focal replication hypotheses include interactions, a 2x3 design, planned contrasts, and an extension outcome. Powering a merged six-cell design from a main-effect Cohen's d taken from a different design does not appropriately justify sensitivity for the actual confirmatory tests.
issues.quote: Given the smallest effect size regarding the effect of intervention (learning identifiable victim effect or not) on donation was found in the original study with Cohens’d = -0.36, the corresponding sample size to detect such effect was 314.

issues.description: The replication replaces consequential monetary giving with an imaginary donation response. This is a major change in the dependent variable: hypothetical willingness to donate is not equivalent to actual donation behavior under real financial cost. Because the original studies used real money donations, this change substantially weakens construct validity and the claim of close replication.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original studies gave participants real money earned from a prior survey, creating a real cost to donation. This replication removes that endowment procedure. Without earned or endowed money, the psychological meaning of the donation choice changes substantially, making the behavior less comparable to the original and potentially inflating prosocial responding.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: Rather than separately replicating Studies 1 and 3, the manuscript merges them into a single 2x3 experiment and additionally applies the explicit intervention to the joint condition. This changes the design logic, condition structure, and interpretation of effects, so the study is not a straightforward direct replication of either original experiment.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly labels the study as a 'close to very close replication' despite multiple substantial departures from the original: hypothetical instead of real donations, online MTurk instead of in-person recruitment, updated stimuli, added measures, changed procedures, and an altered condition structure. This overstates comparability to the target study and risks overstating what a null or positive finding would mean for replication success.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.description: The manuscript equates 'deliberative thinking' with being taught about the identifiable victim effect. This operationalization is conceptually problematic because it may induce demand characteristics, hypothesis guessing, or norm compliance rather than analytic reasoning per se. The manipulation therefore does not cleanly instantiate the theoretical construct it is claimed to test.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.description: The manuscript assumes that presenting victim statistics or teaching participants about the bias activates deliberative thought, but reports no manipulation check or measure of analytic processing, deliberation, comprehension, or bias awareness. Without such verification, failure or success of the manipulation cannot be distinguished from failure of theory.
issues.quote: The victim statistics was believed to eliminate the identifiable victim effect implicitly in the joint condition as reflected in the donation towards the identifiable victim.

issues.description: The paper aggregates conceptually distinct variables into a single 'aggregated feeling' score, including emotions (upset, sympathy, touched) and non-emotional judgments (moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact). This aggregation lacks construct coherence, and no reliability or factor-analytic justification is reported. Any null or significant effect on this composite is therefore hard to interpret.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling ... Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.description: The results interpret a contemporaneous correlation between post-task feelings and donation as testing whether feelings 'predict' donation. Because these variables are measured in the same session and feelings appear to be assessed after the donation decision, the analysis cannot establish temporal precedence or causal prediction. Donation may also influence reported feelings.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: The donation outcome is a bounded 0-5 response and was originally analyzed with ordered probit regression, yet the replication explicitly drops that model and relies on ANOVA. This choice is not justified, and it ignores the ordinal/discrete nature of the dependent variable and possible assumption violations. At minimum, an ordinal or count-sensitive robustness analysis should be reported.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The manuscript conducts a large number of inferential tests across multiple feeling outcomes and effects (identifiability, intervention, interaction for each outcome), yet reports a single p = .045 result without any clear family-wise correction for this analysis family. This materially increases the risk that the lone 'significant' perceived-impact effect is a false positive.
issues.quote: Perceived impact (Extension) | 2 | 3.11 | .006 | [0.00,0.02] | .045*

issues.description: Reported Cohen's d values for post-hoc contrasts appear inconsistent with the corresponding means, standard deviations, and t statistics, suggesting miscalculation or misuse of the effect size metric. For example, the mean difference between identifiable and statistical donation conditions is about 0.30 with SDs around 1.7, which would imply a larger standardized effect than d = 0.076. Similar discrepancies appear for perceived-impact contrasts.

The sign of the reported t statistic for the identifiable-versus-statistical donation contrast conflicts with the narrative interpretation. A negative t for 'Identifiable VS Statistical' would ordinarily indicate lower scores in the identifiable condition if computed in that order, yet the text says identifiable donation was higher. This inconsistency makes the coding/order of the contrast unclear and undermines confidence in the post-hoc reporting.
issues.quote: Identifiable VS Statistical | 994 | -2.40 | 0.13 | 0.076 | [-0.05, 0.20] | .049* ... participants who faced an identifiable victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The abstract claims support for a perceived-impact pattern that is not what the reported results show. The only significant post-hoc difference reported is between the statistical and joint conditions; there is no reported significant difference between identifiable and statistical conditions. The abstract therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the extension findings.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts that identifiable victims will elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims, but the reported significant difference is in the opposite comparison direction (statistical > joint), with no identifiable-versus-statistical effect. This mismatch is not acknowledged as a failed prediction.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.description: The analysis plan states that Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons will be conducted only if identifiability and intervention effects are significant, but the results proceed to post-hoc testing for perceived impact when only identifiability is significant and intervention is not. This departure from the stated decision rule increases researcher degrees of freedom and should be explicitly disclosed and justified.
issues.quote: Bonferroni -adjusted pairwise comparisons  (Note: We conduct the test only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant) ... only the result of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation yielded significant findings. We conducted post-hoc tests to further study the difference of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation.

issues.description: Essential methodological details are not reported in the paper itself. Instead, readers are referred to external links for the full survey and procedure. This prevents evaluation of item wording, scale anchors, manipulation content, consent language, and exact condition materials from the manuscript alone, limiting reproducibility and peer review.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/9sda2czfg6rzko3/AACsg1vIzXhMOInM7XMtV5ILa?dl=0

issues.description: The manuscript advertises open-science materials, but some key fields are incomplete or missing. Missing links and an unfinished preregistration review field make it difficult to verify the preregistration, peer review history, or supporting materials.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> ... Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here> ... OSF pre-registration review:.

issues.description: Random assignment is mentioned, but the manuscript does not report how randomization was implemented, the allocation ratio, whether block/randomization checks were used, or how assignment was embedded in Qualtrics/MTurk. These details are needed to evaluate internal validity and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Participants will be assigned randomly to the intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The extension frames perceived impact of donation as one of the 'feeling variables' and analyzes it alongside affective reactions. Perceived impact is more plausibly a cognitive efficacy appraisal than an affective state, so treating it as an emotional reaction muddies the theoretical distinction between affective and deliberative processes.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the “perceived impact of donation” as one of the feeling variables indicated in Small et al. (2007)’s Study 1.

issues.description: The planned replication uses an online MTurk sample and hypothetical donation judgments rather than in-person participants making real donations. This substantially limits generalization to real charitable behavior and to the original laboratory context, yet the manuscript does not meaningfully qualify its claims on that basis.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania
